body:
Why the Company established courts

Territorial rule required courts to decide disputes, punish offences and apply laws. The Company did not create one uniform judicial structure throughout India at once. It reorganised existing institutions and introduced new courts, especially as its responsibilities in Bengal increased.

Civil and criminal courts under Warren Hastings

In 1772, under Warren Hastings, the Company began reorganising district judicial administration in Bengal. Two important categories were the Diwani Adalat and the Faujdari Adalat.

InstitutionMain responsibilityType of matter
Diwani AdalatCivil justice.Property, inheritance and other civil disputes.
Faujdari AdalatCriminal justice.Offences and criminal proceedings.
Sadar Diwani AdalatHigher civil appellate authority.Appeals in civil matters.
Sadar Nizamat AdalatHigher criminal appellate authority.Appeals in criminal matters.

The district arrangements used both European Company officials and Indian legal specialists. Pandits assisted with the interpretation of Hindu law and maulvis with Islamic law where those traditions applied. Criminal courts also involved officers such as qazis and muftis under the early arrangements.

The word Sadar indicated a superior or principal court. A district court and a Sadar appellate court were therefore not institutions of the same level.

The Supreme Court at Calcutta

The Regulating Act of 1773 authorised the creation of a Supreme Court of Judicature at Fort William in Calcutta, which was established in 1774.

This court was a Crown court, distinct from the Company's Adalat system. It applied English legal procedures within its jurisdiction, while Company courts continued to administer civil and criminal justice through other arrangements. Their overlapping claims of authority produced disputes about which court could hear particular cases.

Two different judicial arrangements

The Company's Diwani and Faujdari Adalats developed as part of its territorial administration. The Supreme Court at Calcutta was established under Crown authority in 1774. The presence of a Supreme Court did not mean that the Company's district courts disappeared.

Cornwallis and judicial reorganisation

The Cornwallis Code of 1793 reorganised judicial administration, particularly in Bengal. It separated revenue collection more clearly from judicial responsibilities and placed regular district judicial functions under judges rather than allowing the revenue collector to decide cases arising from his own administration.

As British territories expanded, courts and judicial arrangements continued to differ by region. The major institutional distinction remained between the executive collection of revenue and the judicial determination of legal disputes.

Law-making and codification

The Charter Act of 1833 centralised legislative authority and provided for a Law Commission. Under Macaulay, the First Law Commission prepared a draft penal code in 1837. The resulting Indian Penal Code was enacted in 1860.

Codification means bringing rules of law together into a systematic written code. It was different from creating a court: a code stated legal rules, whereas courts applied those rules to disputes and offences.

Indian High Courts Act of 1861

The Indian High Courts Act of 1861 empowered the British Crown to establish High Courts by issuing Letters Patent, which were formal royal instruments creating and defining the courts.

High Courts were established at Calcutta, Madras and Bombay in 1862. They brought together functions previously exercised by the Presidency Supreme Courts and the Sadar Adalats. The new courts exercised both original jurisdiction in specified matters and appellate jurisdiction over decisions of lower courts.

The Bombay High Court received its charter on 26 June 1862 and was inaugurated on 14 August 1862. Its creation was important for the judicial administration of the Bombay Presidency, which included directly administered British territories in Gujarat.

The Indian High Courts Act was passed in 1861; the first High Courts at Calcutta, Madras and Bombay were established in 1862. The Act authorised their creation, but the courts were established through separate Letters Patent.

Prelims focus

  • 1772: Warren Hastings's district judicial arrangements in Bengal.
  • Diwani Adalat: civil matters; Faujdari Adalat: criminal matters.
  • Sadar Diwani Adalat: civil appeals; Sadar Nizamat Adalat: criminal appeals.
  • 1774: Supreme Court established at Calcutta.
  • 1837: First Law Commission's draft penal code; 1860: Indian Penal Code enacted.
  • 1861: Indian High Courts Act; 1862: High Courts established at Calcutta, Madras and Bombay.
  • Trap: The Calcutta Supreme Court established in 1774 and the Calcutta High Court established in 1862 were different institutions.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 2, section Setting up a New Administration, printed pp. 21–22, 2020–21 printing; Law Commission of India, Early Beginnings, published 2 July 2018, paragraphs on the First Law Commission and draft Penal Code; Bombay High Court, History, sections The Supreme Court and The Bombay High Court, consulted 20 November 2026; P. J. Griffiths, The British Impact on India, discussion of the Cornwallis judicial reforms.]

title: Judicial Administration: From Adalats to High Courts

body:
What racial hierarchy meant in colonial rule

The British colonial administration organised many opportunities and privileges according to distinctions between Europeans and Indians. Racial hierarchy meant that European identity often carried greater access to senior offices, authority and legal privileges, while Indians faced disadvantages even when they possessed relevant education or experience.

This hierarchy was not identical in every place or period. Some Indians became judges, lawyers and senior officials. Nevertheless, British dominance remained a central feature of the administrative system.

Employment: formal principles and practical barriers

The Charter Act of 1833, through Section 87, declared that a person should not be disqualified from Company employment solely on grounds including religion, place of birth, descent or colour.

Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 similarly promised impartial consideration for qualified subjects seeking government employment, regardless of race or creed. These statements expressed principles of access to office, but they did not remove every barrier.

The higher civil service remained heavily European. After competitive recruitment began, the examination was conducted in London from 1855, in English, with subjects that favoured candidates educated in Britain. Indian candidates also faced the costs of travel and restrictive age requirements.

The success of Satyendranath Tagore, who passed the Indian Civil Service examination in 1863 and joined in 1864, demonstrated that entry was possible. It did not mean that Indians had achieved equal representation or influence in the service.

Racial divisions in colonial towns

British administrative and residential areas sometimes reflected distinctions between Europeans and Indians. In Madras, for example, the area associated with Fort St George developed as a European administrative and residential centre, commonly called White Town. The adjacent Indian settlement came to be known as Black Town.

These were historical labels used in a society marked by colonial racial distinctions. They indicate patterns of residence, authority and privilege rather than two legally uniform categories covering every person or settlement.

Comparable distinctions appeared in other major colonial cities, although their precise boundaries, populations and regulations differed. The important relationship is that political dominance could be reflected in both administrative institutions and urban space.

Unequal justice and the Ilbert Bill controversy

Racial privilege also affected the administration of criminal justice. In parts of British India, qualified Indian judicial officers faced restrictions on trying European British subjects, even when their official rank would otherwise permit them to hear comparable criminal cases.

In 1883, during the viceroyalty of Lord Ripon, a proposal associated with Law Member Courtenay Ilbert sought to remove restrictions based on race from the criminal jurisdiction of qualified Indian judges and magistrates.

The proposal became known as the Ilbert Bill. It provoked strong opposition from sections of the European community in India, who resisted the prospect of European defendants being tried by Indian judicial officers.

A compromise enacted in 1884 did not establish unrestricted equality. It allowed European British defendants before a High Court, Court of Session or District Magistrate to demand a jury with at least half its members European or American, regardless of the presiding judicial officer's race.

What the controversy demonstrated

The Ilbert Bill was concerned with the criminal jurisdiction of qualified Indian judicial officers over European British subjects. It was not a proposal to allow every Indian citizen to act as a judge. The opposition and compromise revealed the continuing importance of racial privilege in colonial justice.

How the institutions fit together

The colonial administrative state developed through related changes. Parliamentary legislation increasingly controlled the Company; the Charter Acts altered its powers; the Crown assumed direct government in 1858; and civil servants, collectors, police officers and judges implemented authority at different levels.

The principal institutional sequence included parliamentary regulation in 1773, stronger political supervision in 1784, major Charter Acts in 1813, 1833 and 1853, Crown rule in 1858, police and High Court legislation in 1861, the first Presidency High Courts in 1862, and the Ilbert Bill controversy in 1883.

These developments introduced more regular offices and legal procedures, but administrative organisation did not itself guarantee racial equality. The same colonial state that introduced competitive recruitment and codified laws also maintained substantial European advantages in employment and justice.

Prelims focus

  • 1833: Section 87 of the Charter Act addressed specified grounds of disqualification from Company employment.
  • 1858: Queen Victoria's Proclamation promised impartial access to qualified government employment.
  • 1855: Indian Civil Service competitive examinations began in London.
  • 1863: Satyendranath Tagore passed the examination; he joined in 1864.
  • White Town and Black Town: historical colonial residential distinctions, notably in Madras.
  • 1883: Ilbert Bill under Lord Ripon; 1884: compromise retaining a special jury provision for European defendants.
  • Trap: A legal declaration against discrimination did not mean that discrimination had disappeared in practice.

[Government of India Act 1833, Section 87, original enacted text, UK legislation archive; Cambridge University Press, The Queen's Urdu: Translating Colonial Secularity in Victoria's 1858 Proclamation, discussion of access to public office; Press Information Bureau, UPSC: A Century of Meritocracy and Inclusion, 30 September 2026, section The Road to 1926; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Class 12, Chapter 12, Colonial Cities, section 4, Segregation, Town Planning and Architecture, printed pp. 331–332; Law and History Review, Volume 42, Issue 4, November 2024, Constitutional Panic in British India: How the Ilbert Bill Controversy of 1883 Revealed the Constitutive Character of Racial Discrimination in the British Empire, sections The Ilbert Bill Proposal in Its Historical Context and The Ilbert Bill Controversy, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A timeline of colonial supervision leads to administrative institutions, then contrasts formal equality promises with racial barriers to power.
pictures.caption: The colonial administrative state combined central legislation, district institutions and unequal access to power.

title: Racial Hierarchy and Unequal Access to Colonial Administration
